passage: At the school gate in Manchester, Marek was tying his shoelaces when nine-year-old Mina called across the pavement, "You live on the estate, don't you? My dad says estate kids are dirty and take things." Marek's face went still. He picked up his bag and walked to the far end of the wall. Mina shrugged, puzzled. That evening her mother heard about it from Marek's mum at the shop. She sat Mina down. "Where did you hear that?" "Dad said it." "It's a hurtful thing to say about people. Marek lives in a flat, like lots of families, and he isn't dirty or a thief. How do you think he felt?" Mina's ears went pink. Next morning she went to Marek. "I'm sorry I said that. It wasn't true."

qa.q: Where did Mina say those words to Marek?
qa.a: Mina said them at the school gate in Manchester.

qa.q: What was Mina feeling when her ears went pink?
qa.a: Mina was embarrassed and ashamed. She was beginning to understand that her words had really hurt Marek.

qa.q: What did Mina's mother do that worked better than shouting?
qa.a: She sat down with Mina, asked where the words came from, explained that they were hurtful and untrue, and asked how Marek felt, so Mina could reach her own apology.

qa.q: How did Marek feel when Mina said it?
qa.a: Hurt. His face went still and he picked up his bag and walked to the far end of the wall.

grounding: A child repeats a class insult heard at home without understanding its weight, and calm correction names the hurt and says people are equal.

passage: During free period in Class 5, Trisha, ten, told Riya loudly, "Your mother sweeps floors, so you're small people. My grandmother says so." The class went quiet. Riya stared at the desk. Nandini, the class teacher, walked over and did not raise her voice. "Trisha, come with me for a moment." In the corridor she asked, "Where did you hear those words?" "At home." "Those words can hurt very much. Riya's mother works hard for her family, just like yours. People are not big or small because of their work. How do you think Riya felt?" Trisha's eyes filled. Back in class Trisha said, "Riya, I'm sorry. I didn't think." Riya nodded slowly. At break, Nandini saw them sharing a mat on the floor.

qa.q: What did Trisha say about Riya's mother?
qa.a: Trisha said, "Your mother sweeps floors, so you're small people."

qa.q: What does it suggest about Trisha's feelings that Trisha's eyes filled?
qa.a: Trisha feels sorry and ashamed, and is only now realising how hurtful the words were. Trisha had repeated them without thinking.

qa.q: Which choice by Nandini worked better than shouting?
qa.a: Nandini took Trisha aside, asked where the words came from, said they hurt and that people are not small because of their work, and asked how Riya felt.

qa.q: How might Riya have felt when Trisha said it, and when Trisha apologised?
qa.a: Hurt and embarrassed at first, since Riya stared at the desk. Riya then nodded slowly at the apology, and later shared a mat, so trust may be returning.

grounding: A child repeats a class insult heard at home without grasping its weight, and a teacher calmly names the hurt and says people are equal.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 3, Monday.
During group work, Sachin, eight, told Lavanya he didn't want to sit next to her and used a word about her family's caste. He said it flatly, the way children repeat something heard at home. Lavanya went red and moved her chair away.
I did not shout. I knelt beside Sachin and asked, "Do you know what that word means?" He shook his head. I said, "It's a word some people use to say a family is lower. That isn't true. It hurt Lavanya. Look at her face."
He looked. His eyes filled. "I heard it at home," he whispered. I said, "Then you can be the one who stops it here."
He said sorry to Lavanya on his own. I sat with Lavanya after, and called both families that afternoon.

qa.q: How old is Sachin?
qa.a: Sachin is eight.

qa.q: What does Sachin's eyes filling suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt ashamed and sorry once he saw the hurt on Lavanya's face and understood what the word meant.

qa.q: Why was the teacher's calm correction better than shouting?
qa.a: It named the hurt, explained the word was untrue, and let Sachin see Lavanya's face, so he understood the weight of it instead of just feeling scared.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel after the teacher sat with her?
qa.a: Lavanya was hurt and embarrassed, but being supported and hearing Sachin's apology may help her feel valued.

grounding: A child repeats a caste insult heard at home without knowing its weight, and a teacher calmly names the hurt and explains that people are equal.

passage:
Dear diary,
Today I did a bad thing and I didn't even know it was bad.
Gopika won the drawing prize. I was jealous. I said, "Your mother is only a maid, so how can you win?" I say "only a maid" because Dadi says it at home about Kamla Bai.
Gopika's face went all crumpled and she ran to the girls' room.
At home I told Papa. I thought he would shout. He didn't. He said, "Lokesh, beta, Kamla Bai works harder than any of us. Gopika's mother too. 'Only' is a word to make people small. Would you like someone to say 'only' about me?"
I felt hot in my ears.
Papa said he'll talk to Dadi too.
Tomorrow I'm going to say sorry to Gopika. And tell her the drawing was really good.
Lokesh

qa.q: What prize did Gopika win?
qa.a: Gopika won the drawing prize.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel when Papa asked if he'd like someone to say "only" about him?
qa.a: Lokesh felt ashamed; his ears went hot as he understood how his words had made Gopika feel small.

qa.q: Why did Papa's calm answer work?
qa.a: Papa didn't shout; he explained that the word "only" makes people small, valued the work of Kamla Bai and Gopika's mother, and helped Lokesh imagine the hurt.

qa.q: What would change if Papa had shouted?
qa.a: Lokesh might only feel scared, not understand why the words hurt, and keep repeating what Dadi says.

grounding: A child repeats a class insult heard at home without grasping its weight, and a calm correction names the hurt and teaches equality.

passage:
In the lane behind the grain market, Asif, nine, was playing marbles when Aadhya came to join. Asif scooped up his marbles. "Nanu says not to play with you. Your father cleans the drains."
Aadhya stood very still. Then she walked away without a word.
Nanu was sitting on the charpai outside the shop. He had heard. Asif expected a scolding, but Nanu called him over quietly.
"Who cleans the drains so the lane doesn't flood?"
"Her abba."
"And is that work dirty, or is it useful?"
Asif thought. "Useful."
"I said a foolish thing once, and you copied it. That's my fault. Now go fix what you broke."
Asif ran after Aadhya with his best blue marble.

qa.q: What did Asif run after Aadhya with?
qa.a: Asif ran after Aadhya with his best blue marble.

qa.q: What might Asif have felt when Nanu called him over quietly?
qa.a: Asif expected a scolding, so he probably felt nervous and a little guilty, sensing he had said something wrong to Aadhya.

qa.q: What did Nanu do that made the correction work?
qa.a: He stayed calm, asked questions so Asif could see the work is useful, admitted his own foolish words, and asked Asif to make amends.

qa.q: How might Aadhya see Asif's apology?
qa.a: She might feel surprised and slowly reassured, though it may take time for the hurt to fade.

grounding: In a small-town lane, a child repeats a class insult heard at home, and an elder calmly corrects it by naming the hurt and the worth of the work.

passage: In a school yard in Porto, Noa pointed at Beatriz's worn trainers. "My uncle says people from the housing blocks are rubbish people." Noa said it the way you might say it could rain. Beatriz's face went stiff, and she walked off to the fence. Their teacher, Senhora Costa, had heard. She did not shout. She crouched beside Noa. "Look at Beatriz by the fence. How do you think those words landed?" Noa looked. "Sad?" "Yes. Where someone lives, or how much money a family has, does not make anyone worth less. Beatriz matters exactly as much as you." Noa scuffed a shoe on the ground. "My uncle says it all the time." "Grown-ups get things wrong too." After the break, Noa offered Beatriz half a custard tart.

qa.q: Who did Noa say uses those words all the time?
qa.a: Noa said the uncle says it all the time.

qa.q: What does Noa's casual tone suggest about how Noa felt saying it?
qa.a: Noa said it casually, like a remark about rain, and only guessed Beatriz felt sad when asked to look; the scuffed shoe suggests Noa then felt embarrassed.

qa.q: Why did Senhora Costa's approach work better than shouting?
qa.a: She stayed calm, got Noa to notice Beatriz's hurt and plainly explained that people are equal, so Noa could learn instead of just feeling scolded.

qa.q: What was it like for Beatriz to hear those words?
qa.a: It stung; her face went stiff and she walked off to the fence, hurt at being called rubbish because of where her family lives.

grounding: It illustrates a child repeating a class insult picked up from an uncle and a teacher's calm correction that names the hurt and explains that people are equal.
